newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Time to buy Singapore shares, analysts say.
newsitem.headline: Time to buy Singapore shares, analysts say.

text.p: Singapore's beleaguered stock market has fallen about as far as it is going to fall and now offers good value to investors, brokers say.
"It's too late to sell. Look for buying opportunities," said Neil Payne, head of research at brokerage ING Barings. "Given the recent sell-off, we think the market is discounted."

Singapore's benchmark Straits Times Industrials Index (STII) closed at 2,075.78 points on Friday, down 2.30 on the day, more than 200 points below the 2,278.85 high hit on January 21 and against a high of over 2,500 in February 1996.
Technical analysts said at the weekend the market was hovering just above a band of support around 2,050 points, a level tested several times but not properly breached for more than two years.
If it were to break down lower, the next stop would be around 1,900 points, they say.
But brokers and economists argue there are several reasons why the STII is unlikely to fall below 2,050 points.
They say the market now looks at best fairly valued in a number of sectors and, more importantly, much safer than some of the other bourses in Southeast Asia.
"Given nervousness about Wall Street, global interest rates and recent experience in Thailand, Singapore's safe haven status comes sharply back into focus," Payne said in a note to clients.

"The Singapore market will continue to attract a premium rating, and we see no reason for the rating to be reduced. Political risk is very low, as is inflation, and interest rates are modest and stable," he said.

Lim Eng Hai, head of research at Singapore brokerage J.M. Sassoon, said recent weakness of the Singapore dollar, which has slipped to around 1.44 to the U.S. dollar from above 1.40 three months ago, also made Singapore stocks attractive.

"That means buying Singapore shares offers the potential upside of not only share prices moving up from the low end of a trading range but also a return of the Singapore dollar to its usual long-term secular uptrend," Lim said.

In a paper published on Friday entitled "Downgrade Malaysia, upgrade Singapore", Lim argued Kuala Lumpur shares would suffer in the medium term from the Malaysian central bank's decision to curb lending for share and property purchases from April 1.

These measures, and fears of a slide on the New York stock market, helped push the Kuala Lumpur Composite Index down 15.73 points on Friday to 1,136.78, sharply below its intra-day high of 1,278.94 seen on February 26.
"The Singapore stock market is looking good not because its fundamentals have suddenly changed for the better but because its relative attractions have improved," Lim wrote.
Mano Sabnani, head of research at DBS Securities, agreed:
"The economic numbers due out in Singapore over the next two months are not going to be good, and any falls in New York will dampen the market here," Sabnani said.

"But the Singapore market is already beginning to find some support and we expect a strong recovery in the local economy in the second half of the year," he said. "We still think 2,500 on the STII is not an unachievable level at some point this year."

ING Barings, Sassoon and DBS all recommend Singapore banks, particularly OUB and OCBC. They also like the marine sector, especially Keppel Corp and SembCorp, which they say have been sold down too far.
